title: From leaf out to leaves off: the effect of rising temperatures on oak's growing season length
content: As a result of the cyclical variability in environmental conditions throughout the year, trees in temperate and boreal latitudes adjust the phenology (ie, the timing) of their physiological and developmental processes to favorable conditions. Trees may tolerate, avoid, or escape unfavorable conditions (Vitasse et al. 2014). For example, evergreen trees tolerate winter temperatures and summer heat and drought partly due to thick cuticles covering their leaves. Trees may also avoid frost- and radiation-related damage during the winter by altering leaf chlorophyll and carotenoid concentrations, downregulating photosynthesis and upregulating photoprotection (Murphy et al. 2025). On the other hand, deciduous species escape freezing damage in leaves by remaining leafless during winter dormancy (Vitasse et al. 2014). This entails the degradation of chlorophyll and recycling of leaf nutrients (leaf senescence) and shedding leaves (leaf fall) during the autumn before freezing temperatures arrive and adjusting the timing in which new leaves are produced (budburst and leaf unfolding) to limit frost damage in the spring (Vitasse et al. 2014).
